snippet.title: 3 ways asyncio.gather breaks concurrent code—and how TaskGroup fixes it
snippet.description:
Your gather code is probably silently returning exceptions as values right now.

asyncio.gather runs multiple coroutines concurrently and returns ordered results. Simple. But add return_exceptions=True and you've got a silent killer: exceptions become list values, not raised exceptions. Your code will crash in production when it never crashed in testing. Python 3.11 introduced TaskGroup to fix this. Structured concurrency means errors propagate immediately, other tasks are cancelled automatically, and you can't accidentally swallow failures. In this video you'll see both APIs side-by-side, understand the footgun, and learn when each is actually appropriate.

⏱ TIMESTAMPS
00:00 Intro — the silent-swallowing problem
00:25 asyncio.gather basics — concurrent, ordered
01:10 The return_exceptions footgun — exceptions as values
01:50 TaskGroup — structured concurrency (Python 3.11+)
02:30 Worked example from async exercises
03:15 When to use which API
03:50 Takeaway — default to TaskGroup

📚 RESOURCES

snippet.title: Python's asyncio.TaskGroup handles errors properly 🔥
snippet.description:
If you write Python async code daily, you've shipped this bug — lost exceptions when one task crashes.

Here's the fix — asyncio.TaskGroup in Python 3.11+ automatically cancels sibling tasks and surfaces ALL errors, not just the first.

This affects every Python developer running concurrent tasks in production. When one API call fails, you want the whole batch to stop — not leave hanging requests.

If you ignore this, you ship silent failures. If you use TaskGroup, you get proper concurrent error boundaries with zero boilerplate.

Follow @codingshorter for a new coding trap or trick every single day.

snippet.title: SpaceX Starship Flight 14 - Launch & Booster Splashdown - LAUNCH STREAM
snippet.description:
NSF coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 14. Starship’s first orbital mission is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately six orbits around the planet over the course of a nearly 10-hour flight, with splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile.
 
The Starship upper stage’s primary objectives include the first orbital insertion maneuver, the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites, a deorbit burn using a single Raptor engine while in space, and a controlled reentry, descent, and splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. Starship will only execute a burn to enter orbit after the flight control team has ensured there is sufficient redundancy on hardware critical to doing the subsequent deorbit burn at the end of the mission.
 
The booster’s primary test objective on Flight 14 will be executing a successful launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and landing burn at an offshore landing point in the Gulf. There have been several modifications to hardware and software to address issues seen on the previous flight.

Why Doesn't asyncio.TaskGroup Wait for the Queue to Finish?

If you’re diving into Python's asyncio module, you might encounter a situation where you want to compute the total time taken for tasks in a queue to be completed. While using asyncio.TaskGroup, it can be confusing to see that your timing code might not reflect the total expected sleep time of your tasks. In this post, we’ll explore this issue and provide a clear solution.

Understanding the Problem

When utilizing the asyncio.TaskGroup, you may find that the tasks seem to finish before you start measuring the total time. In the provided code, the intention is to track how long three worker tasks spend sleeping while processing items from a queue. However, when trying to get the total sleep time, the variable total_slept_for always shows 0 since the timing occurs after the tasks have completed.

Example Code Explanation

In this setup, the timing of how long workers sleep should ideally be captured after all tasks have executed and not before. However, as per the current layout, the timing code is effectively outside the async with block that handles the task group.

The Solution

To properly measure the cumulative sleep time of the tasks being executed, it’s essential to adjust when you initiate the timing and ensure it happens while the tasks are still running. Here’s how to modify your code to achieve this:

Step-by-Step Adjustment

Move Timing Code Inside the async with Block:
Place the timing code just before the await q.join() statement to ensure that you are capturing the duration while the tasks are still running.

Update Total Sleep Time Calculation:

Final Thoughts

By adjusting where you are measuring the time taken, you can accurately capture how long each worker sleeps. This highlights a critical part of programming with asyncio—the timing and handling of asynchronous tasks requires careful consideration of where code is placed within async with statements.

With this solution implemented, you'll get the expected sleep durations that truly reflect what is happening with your task group! Happy coding with Python's asynchronous tools!

snippet.title: Asyncio Evolved: Enhanced Exception Handling with TaskGroup in Python 3.11 — Junya Fukuda

[EuroPython 2023 — Terrace 2A on 2023-07-21]
https://ep2023.europython.eu/session/asyncio-evolved-enhanced-exception-handling-with-taskgroup-in-python-311

With the release of Python 3.11 in October 2022, PEP 654 "Exception Groups and except" was accepted, and asyncio.TaskGroup() was added. This enhancement of exception and cancellation handling has allowed asyncio to evolve more flexibly, addressing the existing issues with asyncio APIs, such as insufficient cancellation and exception handling in asyncio.gather.

In this talk, I would like to discuss the problems of existing asyncio APIs and how the newly introduced asyncio.TaskGroup() solves these issues. Attendees will learn about the improved way of handling exceptions and cancellations using asyncio.TaskGroup(), enabling them to write more efficient and robust asynchronous code with Python 3.11.

snippet.title: Python 3.11 TaskGroup vs asyncio.gather: Which Should You Use? (Episode 3)
snippet.description:
How do you run 10 APIs simultaneously without crashing when one fails? In Episode 3, we master batch concurrency in Python!

We explore the differences between parallel batching with asyncio.gather(), resilient error handling with return_exceptions=True, streaming fast results with asyncio.as_completed(), and the revolution of Structured Concurrency in Python 3.11 using asyncio.TaskGroup.

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS:
0:00 - Batch Concurrency Overview
0:50 - Parallel Batching with asyncio.gather()
2:00 - The Ordered Results Guarantee
3:10 - Resilient Error Handling with return_exceptions=True
4:25 - Streaming Results in Order of Speed with as_completed()
5:45 - What is Structured Concurrency? (The Safety Net Mental Model)
6:55 - Python 3.11 asyncio.TaskGroup in Practice
8:00 - Decision Matrix: When to Use gather vs TaskGroup
8:50 - Summary & Episode 4 Preview

💡 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• asyncio.gather() preserves positional output order matching your input arguments.
• Set return_exceptions=True in gather to prevent a single failure from aborting the entire batch.
• Structured Concurrency (asyncio.TaskGroup) guarantees child tasks cannot outlive their parent scope.
• If one task fails inside a TaskGroup, all remaining sibling tasks are cancelled automatically.

snippet.description:
Calling an async function doesn't run it. It returns a coroutine object. That's the bug you keep hitting.

Learn the exact difference between a coroutine and a Task in Python's asyncio — and why mixing them up is the number-one async bug. snippet.title: Starship's Seventh Flight Test
snippet.description:
The first Starship flight test of 2025 flew with ambitious goals: seeking to repeat our previous success of launching and catching the world’s most powerful launch vehicle while putting a redesigned and upgraded Starship through a rigorous set of flight demonstrations.

It served as a reminder that development testing, by definition, can be unpredictable.

On its seventh flight test, Starship successfully lifted off from Starbase in Texas at 4:37 p.m. CT on Thursday, January 16. For the second time ever, the Super Heavy booster returned to the launch site and was caught by the tower. But before Starship could reach space, a fire developed in the aft section leading to a rapid unscheduled disassembly.

As always, success comes from what we learned, and this flight test will help us improve Starship’s reliability as SpaceX seeks to make life multiplanetary.

snippet.title: Starship's Fifth Flight Test
snippet.description:
Starship’s fifth flight test lifted off on October 13, 2024, with our most ambitious test objectives yet as we work to demonstrate techniques fundamental to Starship and Super Heavy’s fully and rapidly reusable design.

And on our first try, Mechazilla caught the booster.

Following a successful liftoff, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and coast, the Super Heavy booster performed its landing burn and was caught by the chopstick arms of the launch and catch tower at Starbase. Thousands of distinct vehicle and pad criteria had to be met prior to the catch attempt, and thanks to the tireless work of SpaceX engineers, we succeeded with catch on our first attempt.

Prior to catch, Starship executed another successful hot-staging separation, igniting its six Raptor engines and completing ascent into outer space. It coasted along its planned trajectory to the other side of the planet before executing a controlled reentry, passing through the phases of peak heating and maximum aerodynamic pressure, before executing a flip, landing burn, and splashdown at its target area in the Indian Ocean. The flight test concluded at splashdown 1 hour, 5 minutes and 40 seconds after launch.

snippet.title: How to Concurrently Flatten Multiple async Generators in Python
snippet.description:
Learn the idiomatic and efficient way to concurrently consume multiple asynchronous generators in Python using asyncio and TaskGroup.
---
This video is based on the question https://stackoverflow.com/q/79330907/ asked by the user 'Ξένη Γήινος' ( https://stackoverflow.com/u/16383578/ ) and on the answer https://stackoverflow.com/a/79331966/ provided by the user 'jsbueno' ( https://stackoverflow.com/u/108205/ ) at 'Stack Overflow' website. Thanks to these great users and Stackexchange community for their contributions.

Visit these links for original content and any more details, such as alternate solutions, latest updates/developments on topic, comments, revision history etc. For example, the original title of the Question was: How to flatten a bunch of asynchronous generators asynchronously?

Also, Content (except music) licensed under CC BY-SA https://meta.stackexchange.com/help/licensing
The original Question post is licensed under the 'CC BY-SA 4.0' ( https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ ) license, and the original Answer post is licensed under the 'CC BY-SA 4.0' ( https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ ) license.

If anything seems off to you, please feel free to drop me a comment under this video.
---
Introduction

When scraping multiple webpages or processing multiple asynchronous data streams in parallel, you might face the challenge of flattening multiple asynchronous generators into a single unified stream of results in real-time.

The Problem

You have many asynchronous generators — each yielding multiple items over time. You want to:

Process all these generators concurrently, not one after another.

Collect items as soon as any generator yields them (no batch waiting).

Get a flattened list of all results.

Naively async for-looping over generators sequentially or using asyncio.gather on async generators does not work as desired, since they await whole generators or coroutines, losing concurrency on intermediate yields.



Why Simple Methods Fail

asyncio.gather and asyncio.as_completed expect coroutines or awaitables, not async generators.

async for sequentially consumes each generator, resulting in total runtime summing all generators' durations.

You want to interleave yields across generators as soon as they happen.

The Right Approach: Concurrent Tasks Consuming Each Async Generator

The core technique is:

Wrap each async generator consumption (async for) inside its own async function.

Schedule all these functions concurrently as independent tasks.

Collect results into a shared list as they arrive.

Example (Python 3.11+  ) Using asyncio.TaskGroup

[[See Video to Reveal this Text or Code Snippet]]

How it works: each consume task independently iterates over one async generator. All run concurrently inside TaskGroup. Results are appended to the shared results list as soon as each item becomes available.

Benefits:

Starts all generators simultaneously.

Items appear as soon as ready (no waiting for completion).

Flattened output with real concurrency.



Alternative: Driving Async Generators Manually with anext

If your Python version is   3.11 or you want finer control, you can anext each generator separately:

Create tasks that await the anext() of each generator.

When a task completes, collect the item and schedule fetching the next item from the same generator.

Repeat until all generators are exhausted.

[[See Video to Reveal this Text or Code Snippet]]

This method is more complex but useful if you require fine-grained control.



Summary

To concurrently flatten multiple async generators in Python:

Wrap each async generator iteration (async for) in an async function.

Use asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+  ) or manage tasks manually.

Aggregate yielded data immediately for fast streaming.

This approach allows you to efficiently consume multiple asynchronous streams without waiting for each to finish, giving you a real-time flattened stream of results.



Final Notes

If you only need the entire result of each generator once complete, asyncio.gather on coroutines returning lists is simpler.

For true streaming and interleaved async results, task-wrapping is the recommended method.

This pattern is invaluable for web scraping, real-time data processing, and any asynchronous data aggregation scenario.

snippet.title: Python's TaskGroup handles 10 concurrent failures cleanly 🔥
snippet.description:
If you write Python async code daily, you've felt the pain of one task failing and silently breaking your entire concurrent workflow.

Here's the fix — asyncio.TaskGroup in Python 3.11+ automatically cancels all tasks when one fails and surfaces every exception.

This affects anyone running concurrent API calls, database queries, or parallel I/O operations where failure isolation matters.

Without TaskGroup, you're managing cancellation and exception gathering manually with gather() — verbose, error-prone, and easy to get wrong in production.

Follow @codingshorter for a new coding trap or trick every single day.

snippet.title: SpaceX Starship Flight 13 - Launch & Landing
snippet.description:
Starship launches Flight 13, the second launch of the Block 3 vehicle from Pad 2 at Starbase. This is the third attempt following a T-0 abort on July 16, and a weather scrub on July 23.

Launch Window: July 24th at 5:45PM to 7:15PM CDT (22:45-00:15 UTC)

Mission: Starship's 13th integrated flight test. Correcting issues from version 3's debut flight.
Launch location: Pad 2, Starbase, Earth. 
Target orbit: Trans-atmospheric
Booster: B20-1
Ship: S40-1
Booster recovery: Expended - will attempt a water splashdown, no recovery.
Ship recovery: Expended - will attempt a water splashdown, no recovery.
Rocket trajectory: Southeast passing between Cuba and the Yucatan Peninsula.
Payload onboard: 20 Starlink v3 satellites, 6 of them fitted with a suite of cameras for heatshield inspection.
Payload mass: ~34 metric tons
Stats:
  - SpaceX's 696th launch overall
  - SpaceX's 87th launch this year
  - SpaceX's 9th launch of the month
  - Starship's 13th launch overall
  - SpaceX's 2nd launch from Pad 2 at Starbase

snippet.title: Python's asyncio.TaskGroup kills scattered error handling ⚡
snippet.description:
If you write Python async code daily, you've written this: try-except blocks around every single asyncio.gather call, manual cancellation on first error, scattered cleanup logic.

Here's the fix — asyncio.TaskGroup in Python 3.11+ handles concurrent task errors properly with automatic cancellation and cleanup.

This affects every Python developer running multiple async tasks in parallel — API calls, database queries, file operations.

Without TaskGroup, one failed task leaves others running orphaned, errors get swallowed, and cleanup becomes your problem.

snippet.title: Solving the TypeError in asyncio TaskGroup with Python 3.11
snippet.description:
Learn how to properly return lists using the `TaskGroup` feature in Python 3.11's asyncio library and fix common pitfalls.

If anything seems off to you, please feel free to write me at vlogize [AT] gmail [DOT] com.
---
Understanding the TypeError in asyncio TaskGroup

Using asynchronous programming allows developers to write non-blocking code and manage tasks efficiently in Python. With the introduction of Python 3.11, the asyncio library now includes a feature called TaskGroup which simplifies task management within an asynchronous context. However, many users have encountered issues, such as TypeError, when trying to return values from tasks. In this guide, we will explore how to resolve these errors and use the TaskGroup correctly.

The Problem

You've written an async function using the new TaskGroup feature, but you're running into a TypeError when attempting to return lists from your tasks. The Python error message states:

[[See Video to Reveal this Text or Code Snippet]]

This indicates there are some syntactical and logical errors in your implementation, which we will resolve step-by-step.

The Code Breakdown

Let’s analyze the provided code and the issues it contains. Here's the original code snippet:

[[See Video to Reveal this Text or Code Snippet]]

Issues Found

Incorrect Use of async with: The async with statement must be followed by asyncio.TaskGroup() to create an instance, not just asyncio.TaskGroup. This throws the TypeError you faced.

Await Behavior: In your squares function, you're trying to use await on a list comprehension. This is incorrect because you aren't dealing with an async call, leading to a logical error that prevents your code from functioning as expected.

Returning Task Objects Instead of Results: In squares_tasks, you're returning the task objects squares1 and squares2, but not the results of these tasks. You need to retrieve results like squares1.result() after the tasks are complete.

The Fixed Code

After addressing the aforementioned issues, here's how your code should look:

[[See Video to Reveal this Text or Code Snippet]]

Key Takeaways

Create TaskGroup Instances: Always ensure that you create an instance using parentheses asyncio.TaskGroup() and not just asyncio.TaskGroup.

Ensure To Get Results: Use the .result() method on your task objects outside the async with block to retrieve the outcomes after all tasks have completed.

Debugging Async Code: Debug asynchronous code by checking not just syntax but the proper await patterns and how results are retrieved.

By following these guidelines, you can effectively use the TaskGroup functionality in Python 3.11’s asyncio library. Happy coding!

snippet.title: Python Level 4 (Master): Patterns, Asyncio, Metaprogramming & Production APIs
snippet.description:
Level 4 of the Python Mastery Path is where you stop learning syntax and start learning how professionals actually ship Python. This video stitches five Master-level lessons into one narrative arc: reusable design patterns (factory, strategy, observer, singleton), structured concurrency with asyncio.TaskGroup and friends, the metaclass machinery that powers real frameworks, hardening a FastAPI service with JWT auth and middleware, and the fixture/mocking/property-testing toolkit that keeps it all honest in CI. Every code example is pulled directly from the source lessons -- nothing invented, nothing simplified past the point of usefulness.

Lessons covered in this video:
- 01 · Design Patterns in Python -- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-4/01-design-patterns/
- 02 · Advanced Asyncio Patterns -- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-4/02-advanced-asyncio/
- 03 · Metaprogramming -- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-4/03-metaprogramming/
- 04 · Production-Grade APIs -- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-4/04-production-apis/
- 05 · Testing at Scale -- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-4/05-testing-at-scale/
